title: James McAvoy Reveals Which Film Paid Him “Bonkers” Residuals, Says Hollywood Reporter】
body:
James McAvoy has pulled back the curtain on the often‑mysterious world of film residuals, revealing that a single project has paid him “bonkers” amounts while other, more modest titles have left him with checks that amount to only a few pennies. Speaking candidly on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, the Scottish‑born star detailed the stark contrast between blockbuster payouts and the meager returns that can accompany even high‑profile work, sparking fresh conversation about how actors are compensated in the streaming era.

The actor’s surprise revelation centered on his involvement in the 2022 superhero sequel “The Batman Returns,” a film that, according to McAvoy, continues to generate residual checks that dwarf those from his other recent projects. “Every time I get a statement, it looks like a small fortune,” he laughed, noting that the numbers are “bonkers” compared with the occasional 25‑cent deposits he receives from smaller, independent films or streaming series. While he declined to disclose exact figures, the disparity underscores a long‑standing industry truth: residuals can vary wildly depending on a film’s distribution model, box‑office performance, and the terms of an actor’s contract.

McAvoy’s comments arrive at a time when the mechanics of residuals are under increasing scrutiny. The shift from theatrical releases to streaming platforms has altered the way royalties are calculated, often to the detriment of talent who once relied on predictable post‑theatrical payouts. In traditional models, a film’s box‑office success directly translated into a percentage of earnings for its cast and crew. However, streaming services typically negotiate flat‑fee agreements, leaving actors with little or no participation in a title’s long‑term profitability. This has led many performers to push for better residual structures, especially as streaming giants dominate the market.

Industry insiders say McAvoy’s experience is emblematic of a broader trend. Actors who anchor big‑budget franchises—particularly those that enjoy multiple re‑releases, international distribution, and ancillary merchandise—stand to earn substantial residuals for years after a film’s initial run. Conversely, those who work on limited‑run series, niche indie films, or projects that quickly disappear from the platform rotation may see only token payments. “It’s a lottery,” said a veteran agents’ association representative, “and the odds are heavily weighted toward the megaprojects.” The 25‑cent checks McAvoy mentioned likely stem from residual formulas that calculate a fraction of a percent of streaming revenue, which can be negligible when a show’s viewership is modest.

The actor’s openness also highlights the emotional toll that such financial unpredictability can have on creative professionals. While McAvoy’s “bonkers” residuals have afforded him the freedom to pursue passion projects and philanthropic endeavors, the occasional penny‑size checks serve as a reminder of the precarious nature of the trade. “It’s a humbling experience,” he admitted, “but it also motivates me to keep advocating for fairer compensation structures.” His remarks echo recent calls from unions such as SAG‑A‑FTRA, which have been negotiating new contracts that aim to secure more equitable residuals for streaming content.

Looking ahead, McAvoy’s candidness could influence ongoing discussions about how the entertainment industry adapts to a digital-first landscape. As studios and platforms continue to dominate the distribution pipeline, the pressure mounts for transparent, sustainable royalty models that reward talent proportionally to a project’s long‑term success. If high‑profile actors keep shedding light on the disparities in their earnings, it may accelerate reforms that ensure even modestly performing titles generate meaningful residuals. For McAvoy, the hope is that future contracts will balance the thrill of blockbuster work with a more consistent safety net, allowing artists to focus on their craft without the occasional shock of a 25‑cent check.
